extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy; readers of Kant's Groundwork
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Kant's arguments in the Groundwork/Metaphysics of Morals concerning pure practical reason, the moral law, freedom, and the distinction between morality and happiness. The text articulates the conditions under which actions have moral worth and how practical reason postulates freedom and a supersensible order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy of a priori moral principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme practical principle (the moral law) is "a law completely a priori and not depending on any sensible data."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant insists moral principles must be independent of empirical sensible data. Any principle that depends on contingent feelings or empirical incentives cannot serve as the supreme practical principle. The text contrasts how theoretical a priori cognition is established by examples in science, while practical a priori must be verified by common practical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of inclination/feeling from moral principle
rubrics_metrics.description: "Pure practical reason positively refuses to admit this feeling [pleasure or pain] into its principle as a condition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an empirical feeling (pleasure, desire, pain) determines the will, the maxim is not pure practical law. Kant gives the procedural test: present the moral law to an empirically-motivated will (e.g., the man tempted to lie for gain); if the moral law separates from the empirical attraction and commands truthfulness, the empirical principle is shown to be heterogeneous and excluded. Mixing feelings with the moral principle is explicitly flagged as an anti-pattern that undermines moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between doctrine of happiness and doctrine of morality
rubrics_metrics.description: In the doctrine of happiness empirical principles constitute the entire foundation, while in that of morality they "do not form the smallest part of it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant requires strict separation: principles motivated by happiness (skill, wealth, means to fulfil duties) may be permissible as instrumental, but cannot be immediate foundations of duty. Taking happiness as the principle of all duty would destroy moral certainty, analogous to empirically mixing with geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity requirement for moral worth (no empirical admixture)
rubrics_metrics.description: All determining principles of the will, except the law of pure practical reason, are empirical and must be kept apart from the supreme principle of morality; incorporation of empirical conditions 'would be to destroy all moral worth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting from duty (the moral law) alone confers moral worth. If empirical motives are conditions for the maxim, the action loses genuine moral worth. Kant's salt/alkali analogy illustrates testing purity: add the moral law and empirical attractions 'precipitate' away when reason is properly legislating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of practical freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical freedom may be defined as 'independence of the will on anything but the moral law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom for moral purposes is independence from empirical determinants. This is not a psychological freedom (internal chains of ideas) but transcendental independence on all empirical conditions. For moral imputation and law, this stronger sense of freedom is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law postulates freedom (practical justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although we cannot demonstrate the possibility of freedom empirically, 'by the moral law which postulates it, [we are] compelled and therefore authorized to assume it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant treats the moral law as a practical postulate: it authorizes assuming supersensible freedom necessary for moral responsibility. This is not theoretical proof but a practical warrant for the concept of freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incompatibility of physical causality with transcendental freedom unless phenomenon/noumenon distinction held
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of nature (causality in time) pertains only to appearances (phenomena); to retain freedom we must regard the subject as a thing in itself (noumenon) not wholly determined by time-conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues that if all existence in time were existence of things in themselves, freedom would be impossible. The rescue is to separate the modal/causal status of appearances from the noumenal self, allowing the same subject to be deterministically bound as phenomenon and free as noumenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendental freedom as condition of moral imputation/responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Without transcendental freedom (independence on everything empirical) 'no moral law and no moral imputation are possible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility and moral blame presuppose that actions can be imputed to a subject not fully determined by empirical causes. Psychological or comparative freedom (internal deterministic chain) is insufficient for moral accountability in Kant's view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of conscience as internal judicial faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience issues moral self-judgement; even when one tries to excuse an unlawful act as oversight or necessity, the 'accuser within' often cannot be silenced if one was 'in possession of his freedom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant uses the persistence of moral self-reproach and repentance as experiential evidence of moral law's authority and the subject's awareness of freedom. Attempts to explain wrongdoing solely by physical necessity are inadequate to silence conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of saying 'I could have done otherwise' despite deterministic appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational being can justly say of every unlawful action that he 'could very well have left it undone' although as appearance it is sufficiently determined in the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant distinguishes judgement from metaphysical determinism: as noumenal, the agent imputes causality to himself and judges actions by moral law, thereby asserting that actions were avoidable in the practical sense even if phenomenally determined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideality of time/space required to reconcile creation and freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: If existence in time is a mere sensible mode of representation, then creation concerns noumena and cannot be equated with being the cause of appearances; this separation is necessary to preserve freedom against the claim that divine creation would make us mere automata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant's solution to the problem that God's causal involvement would undermine freedom is to hold that time/space are forms of sensibility: creation relates to noumenal existence, so divine causality does not entail that God is the author of empirical actions. Rejecting this ideality leads toward deterministic systems like Spinozism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law as unconditioned practical principle providing objective reality of supersensible causality
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral law is the incontestable objective principle of causality which excludes all sensible conditions: 'that unconditioned causality... is the principle of morality' and thereby establishes the reality of the supersensible world for practical purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues that practical reason can legitimately posit an intelligible, unconditioned causality grounded in the moral law. This gives practical (not speculative) knowledge of a supersensible order and justifies speaking of the self as partly noumenal.
